newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco deal possible this week - Moore.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco deal possible this week - Moore.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

A key negotiator in tobacco talks said Monday he was hopeful a settlement will be reached this week but warned that stumbling blocks remain and that the first state trial against the industry was still scheduled.

"We're hopeful we'll bring this thing to resolution this week but again we have some real tough details to deal with and they are very important to the public health of this country," Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore said.
"I really think we'll come to a resolution this week if at all humanly possible," he told reporters.
Moore said he thought negotiations would continue through Tuesday or Wednesday. He said he expected Monday's talks to last until midnight or early Tuesday morning.

Sources close to the talks that one of the most contentious issues that still remains is whether individuals would be able to sue for punitive damages, which are awarded to punish and deter wrongful behavior.
They said state officials might send a draft proposal to the White House without the punitive damage issue resolved since both sides had already agreed to a number of health care provisions.

Under those terms, the tobacco industry has agreed to sharply curtail advertising and stop using cartoon characters, pay penalties if youth smoking is not reduced over certain time periods, and to pay for cessation programs.
Moore was asked if a lack of agreement on the punitive damage issue could kill the deal.

"I don't think the people of this country would let this resolution fall apart because, frankly, what's been achieved so far is more than anyone in the public health community has ever imagined," Moore said.

However, he said that even if a preliminary agreement was reached, he would still go forward with his July 7 trial against tobacco companies. Moore is one of 37 state attorneys general that have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid health costs of sick smokers.

"I am not going to move my trial," he said. "If there is a final resolution and I've seen the ink and it's dry and there are commitments from everyone there needs to be commitments from, I'll think about it, but I don't have any intention to move my case."

Moore spoke to reporters after a meeting at the White House where he briefed Bruce Lindsey, a senior adviser to President Bill Clinton, about progress in negotiations. He said the White House is now being updated daily.
"They're indicating publicly that they are into critical stages of their talks and they routinely come by," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said.
When asked to describe the role of the White House in the talks, McCurry said: "Still the same. Keeping an eye on it. We've given them our tentative reactions to elements of their discussions."
Also Monday, Rep. Henry Waxman, a California Democrat, was invited to the White House and met with Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles to discuss how to proceed in Congress if there were a settlement.

The attorneys general, the highest ranking legal officers of each state, and the tobacco industry have been negotiating since early April to try to settle huge claims against the industry and resolve major public health issues.

As the talks continued in Washington, the legal battle against the tobacco industry was set to spread to Canada. On Monday, British Columbia announced legislation paving the way for the province to become the first in Canada to sue tobacco companies to recoup medical costs for treating smokers.

The province is believed to be the first government outside the United States to pursue such action against tobacco manufacturers. Several other Canadian provinces and the Canadian federal government are considering similar steps, officials said.

"The legal battle against the tobacco industry is spreading as governments not only in the United States but worldwide believe this is a battle that should be fought and won," said British Columbia Health Minister Joy MacPhail.
Before British Columbia files its lawsuit, the government said it was first asking the tobacco industry to compensate it voluntarily for tobacco-related illness and smoking prevention programs.
